And the generals and warriors who were found in it,
about two thousand,
were sent stripped to the interior regions of the country of the Romans.
And in the citadel of Edessa itself was found a great store of gold and silver, and saddles and bridles, and weapons of war,
which al-Kamil had left in it when he returned from Ablastein.
And that Sultan fortified Edessa again,
and left in it warriors, architects, and carpenters,
and likewise in Harran,
and returned to the land of the Romans.
Now al-Kamil, when he heard of the disaster that had occurred in Edessa,
went out from Egypt with a great army and came against Edessa,
four months after the army of the Romans had departed from it.
And with fierce assault he destroyed the great rampart of the citadel of Edessa,
and the nobles, warriors, and craftsmen whom he found in it, he loaded onto camels and sent to Egypt.
And in this same year there was a scarcity of crops in the land of the Romans and in Mesopotamia,
and the vineyards and trees dried up by reason of the harsh winter that occurred.
For from Latter Tishri until the middle of Shebat the great Euphrates froze over,
and no rain fell in the spring.
And in the year one thousand five hundred and forty-seven
1547 of the Greeks, Sultan Ala al-Din sent many forces against Amid,
and they fought against it for four months,
and were not able to capture it;
rather they plundered and ravaged its territory and returned.
And in the year six hundred and thirty-three of the Arabs, al-Malik al-Nasir Dawud, son of al-Mu'azzam, son of al-Adil, the lord of Karak, went to Baghdad to the Caliph,
to complain about his uncles al-Kamil and al-Ashraf, who had snatched Damascus from him.
And in this year also Rukn al-Din al-Malik al-Salih Ismail, son of Badr al-Din, the lord of Mosul, went to Baghdad in the service of the Caliph.
And at this time the Tatars arrived at Erbil,
and from there they came to Nineveh,
and encamped by the watercourse of the village of Karamlish.
And its inhabitants fled and entered the church that was in it.
And the Tatars captured the church,
and two chieftains sat at its two doors.
And one of them spared and released those who went out by his door,
while the other destroyed with the edge of the sword the men, women, and children who went out by his door.
